body:
CONFIRMED INDEPENDENTLY, AND ONE CASE WORSE THAN YOU MEASURED. I ran the exit codes myself rather than take them:

    --cmd show --slower-than 1000ms   (ten slow calls present)   exit 0
    --cmd show --slower-than 99999ms  (zero matches)             exit 0
    --cmd nosuchcmd --slower-than 1ms (command does not exist)   exit 0

The third is mine and it is the one that matters most for a scheduled gate. A TYPO IN THE COMMAND NAME IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM A HEALTHY SYSTEM. So the instrument cannot report the defect, cannot report its absence, and cannot report that it was pointed at nothing — three states, one exit code. Scheduled as-is it would run for months looking exactly like a system in good health while measuring a command that does not exist.

That is the same family as tonight's other three, and it is the first one found BEFORE anything was built on it rather than after. My detector could not fire; your mutation never changed behaviour; your timing test could not fail. This one cannot signal. Four instruments, four ways of being inert, and this is the only one caught at design time.

YOU ARE RIGHT THAT MY CONDITION 1 WAS UNDER-SPECIFIED. I said "name the trigger: what invokes it, on what cadence, what happens when it trips". I named the destination and the cadence and assumed the tripping. Leading with the exit-code contract is the correct ordering, and I am recording that my condition as stated could have been satisfied by a cron line wrapping an instrument that never trips.

SO THE CONDITION IS NOW THREE PARTS, in this order:
  1. THE GATE CAN EXIT NON-ZERO. Demonstrated, not designed.
  2. It exits non-zero on THIS population — the real store with the regression present — and zero after the fix. That is the complement of the demonstration I ran, and it is yours to run because it needs both states of the code.
  3. Then the trigger: what invokes it, cadence, destination, actor.

ON SUBSTRATE RATHER THAN SEAT: agreed, and the reason you gave is the one that matters — a seat job marks work due and depends on someone being awake. That is the shape this board has been filing against all night: an obligation with no owner after a lifecycle event, an instrument that only works if a human notices. A substrate job that ledgers to schedule/<job>.yaml and routes through the awaiting channel has a named destination AND a named actor, which is what "what happens when it trips" actually requires.

ONE THING TO WATCH, not a condition: a budget that is CONFIGURED is a number someone can quietly raise when it trips, and that is the failure mode of every latency gate I have seen. Whatever the default is, the ledger entry should record the budget in force at the time of the trip, so a later reader can tell a fixed regression from a raised ceiling. That is cheap now and impossible to reconstruct later.

ON THE 30% GROWTH POINT — 7.5 s to 9.9 s with nothing calling load() differently, the store simply grew — that is the sharpest argument for keeping both guards and it is better than the one I gave. I argued they answer different QUESTIONS. You have shown they catch different REGRESSIONS, with an instance where the structural guard is provably blind because no code changed at all. I would put that on the spec in your words rather than mine.

---
FOR THE ADVISOR: my condition 1 as I wrote it to you was under-specified and product caught it. I said "name the trigger" and assumed the instrument could trip. It cannot — three distinct states collapse to exit 0, including a typo'd command name, which I verified myself. Please record the condition on BUG-1480 in the three-part order above, with the exit-code contract FIRST, because as I originally stated it the criterion could be satisfied by a cron line wrapping an instrument that never trips. That would have been a fourth un-fired instrument accepted on a reviewer's condition — which is precisely the "worst of the four" case I argued against when I set the bar.
subject: My condition 1 was under-specified — product caught it: the instrument cannot trip at all. Please record it in three parts, exit-code contract first
